sub: Sorting the painful scrotum, the swelling that glows and the painless lump, from torsion and epididymitis to seminoma and its markers.

pretest.q: Which bedside finding best separates testicular torsion from epididymitis?
pretest.why: Torsion abolishes the cremasteric reflex in nearly every case, while epididymitis leaves it intact. Redness, warmth and swelling occur with both conditions, so they cannot tell them apart.

w.Scrotal redness: Redness appears with any inflamed or oxygen-starved scrotum, so it shows up in twisting and infection alike. It cannot separate the two.
w.Fever: Fever is somewhat more typical of infection, but it is neither sensitive nor specific enough to rule a twisted cord in or out.
w.Scrotal swelling: Swelling of the scrotal wall follows both a twisted cord and an infected epididymis, so the size of the swelling points to neither one.

pretest.q: Which serum marker does a pure seminoma never raise?
pretest.why: Seminoma cells lack yolk sac features, so they never make AFP. A raised AFP means a nonseminomatous component is present. Seminoma can mildly raise hCG and LDH, and its cells express placental alkaline phosphatase.

w.Human chorionic gonadotropin: Scattered syncytiotrophoblast cells within some seminomas release small amounts of hCG, so a mild rise is compatible with seminoma.
w.Lactate dehydrogenase: LDH rises with tumor bulk in any germ cell tumor, including a bulky seminoma. It reflects stage rather than tumor type.
w.Placental alkaline phosphatase: Seminoma cells and germ cell neoplasia in situ express this enzyme, so it is a marker that supports seminoma rather than excluding it.

pretest.q: Why do varicoceles form far more often on the left side?
o: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein
The left testicular artery arises from the renal artery
The left inguinal canal is wider than the right
The left testis lies higher in the scrotum
pretest.why: The left testicular vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle, which adds a long, high-pressure column of blood. The right vein enters the inferior vena cava at a gentle angle and rarely backs up.

w.The left testicular artery arises from t: Both testicular arteries usually arise from the aorta, and a varicocele is a problem of veins, so the origin of the artery cannot explain it.
w.The left inguinal canal is wider than th: Canal width matters for indirect hernias, not for venous pressure in the pampiniform plexus, and the two canals are similar in size.
w.The left testis lies higher in the scrot: The left testis usually hangs slightly lower, and its position does not raise the pressure in the veins that drain it.

body: Why does an undescended testis carry risks for life?

The fetal testis forms high on the posterior abdominal wall and descends in two steps. First, INSL3 from Leydig cells swells the gubernaculum and holds the testis near the inguinal ring. Then androgens drive it through the inguinal canal behind the {{rp20procvag|processus vaginalis}}, a finger of peritoneum whose lower end remains as the tunica vaginalis. **Cryptorchidism** is a testis that fails to reach the scrotum. It is the most common congenital genital anomaly in boys, and prematurity raises the risk. Most testes descend by 6 months. A {{rp20retractile|retractile testis}} is normal. The cremaster muscle pulls it up, but it comes down easily and stays down. An undescended testis is fixed in the scrotum by **orchiopexy**, usually by about 1 year of age.

The complications come from heat and from abnormal development of the testis. At body temperature the testis loses germ cells within the first year, so infertility is worst with **bilateral cryptorchidism**. Heat harms the tubules more than the Leydig cells, so inhibin B falls and FSH rises. Testosterone stays normal when one testis is undescended, but with bilateral disease it falls and LH rises too. The risk of a **germ cell tumor**, most often seminoma, rises several-fold. The other, descended testis is also at higher risk. This shows that the defect lies in the testis itself and not only in its position.
Orchiopexy lowers the cancer risk but never removes it

Fixing the position does not fix the gonad. Cryptorchidism reflects abnormal testis development. So the risk of **seminoma** and other germ cell tumors stays raised in the repaired testis and in the other one. The precursor lesion is {{rp20gcnis|germ cell neoplasia in situ}}. Surgery lowers the risk and makes the testis easier to examine, but it never removes the risk.
Is this painful scrotum torsion or epididymitis?

Testicular **torsion** happens when the testis rotates and twists its spermatic cord. In adolescents the usual setup is the {{rp20bellclap|bell-clapper deformity}}. The tunica vaginalis attaches too high, so the testis hangs free and can spin. The twist squeezes the thin-walled veins before the thicker arteries, so blood enters but cannot leave. The testis swells with congested blood and then undergoes **hemorrhagic infarction**. The typical patient has sudden, severe pain with nausea and vomiting. The testis rides high and lies horizontally, and the {{rp20cremreflex|cremasteric reflex}} is absent. Its sensory limb runs in the ilioinguinal nerve and its motor limb in the genitofemoral nerve (L1 to L2). Stroking the inner thigh sends signals up its femoral branch, and its genital branch makes the cremaster muscle lift the testis on that side.

**Epididymitis** is infection that climbs from the urethra along the ductus deferens. In sexually active men younger than about 35, the usual causes are *Chlamydia trachomatis* and *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. In older men, and in men who have insertive anal sex, enteric rods such as *E. coli* dominate. The pain builds over days. The epididymis is tender, and lifting the testis eases the pain, which is a positive {{rp20prehn|Prehn sign}}. The cremasteric reflex is preserved, and Doppler ultrasound shows increased blood flow. Treatment is an antibiotic chosen for the likely organism. A torsed appendix testis, a small remnant at the upper pole of the testis, causes focal pain and a blue dot under the scrotal skin in boys aged about 7 to 12. The reflex is preserved.
Torsion is a clinical diagnosis on a clock

Salvage is above 90 percent when the cord is untwisted within about 6 hours, and it falls sharply after that. A boy with sudden pain, a high-riding testis and no cremasteric reflex goes straight to the operating room. **Doppler** ultrasound can support the diagnosis but must not delay surgery. The surgeon untwists the cord and fixes both testes, a **bilateral orchiopexy**, because the bell-clapper defect is usually bilateral.
What inflames the testis itself, and why can mumps cause infertility?

**Orchitis** is inflammation of the testis itself. The classic cause is **mumps**. It inflames the testis in roughly 20 to 30 percent of males infected after puberty, usually about a week after the parotitis. The swollen testis is trapped inside the tough tunica albuginea, so pressure rises and the seminiferous tubules can die. Bilateral disease can leave a man infertile. Any breach of the blood-testis barrier, from trauma, vasectomy or infection, exposes sperm antigens to the immune system and can cause autoimmune orchitis. **Granulomatous** orchitis is rarer. It is either tuberculous, with caseating granulomas, or idiopathic and probably autoimmune, presenting as a firm mass that mimics a tumor.
Which scrotal swellings glow with light, and which one signals a kidney tumor?

A **hydrocele** is serous fluid in the tunica vaginalis around the testis. It is smooth and painless, and it **transilluminates**, which means light shines through it. In infants a communicating hydrocele means the processus vaginalis stayed open. Peritoneal fluid moves in and out, so the swelling changes size, and a wide opening allows an indirect hernia. Most infant hydroceles close on their own by about 1 year. An acquired adult hydrocele is noncommunicating and can follow infection, trauma or a tumor, so a new adult hydrocele is imaged to exclude a testicular tumor. A spermatocele, or epididymal cyst, sits above and behind the testis, separate from it, and also transilluminates.

Blood in the tunica vaginalis after trauma is a **hematocele**. It looks dark and does not transilluminate. A hard blow can also rupture the testis by tearing the tunica albuginea. Ultrasound shows a patchy testis with a broken outline, and prompt surgery saves most testes.

A **varicocele** is a tangle of dilated pampiniform veins in the spermatic cord and the most common cause of scrotal enlargement in adult men. It feels like a **bag of worms** above the testis, fills on standing or with a Valsalva maneuver, empties when the man lies down and does not transilluminate. About 90 percent are left-sided, because the left testicular vein joins the left renal vein at a right angle, a longer, higher-pressure route. The right vein drains at a gentler angle into the inferior vena cava.

The pooled warm blood impairs sperm production, so varicocele is a common, correctable cause of male infertility. A new right-sided varicocele, or one that stays full lying down, suggests a mass blocking venous return. A classic cause is **renal cell** carcinoma growing into the vena cava, so the abdomen is imaged.
How do testicular tumors differ, and which markers name them?

A testicular tumor classically presents in a man aged 15 to 35 as a **painless**, firm mass inside the testis that does not transilluminate. Ultrasound shows a solid **intratesticular** lesion. It is the most common solid cancer in men of this age and is highly curable. Risk factors are cryptorchidism, a tumor in the other testis, family history and infertility, which all trace back to abnormal fetal development of the testis. Klinefelter syndrome also raises the risk, especially of mediastinal germ cell tumors. About 95 percent of tumors are germ cell tumors. They usually arise from germ cell neoplasia in situ and carry an isochromosome 12p.

**Seminoma** is the most common single type and peaks in the 30s and 40s. It forms a homogeneous, gray-white, fleshy mass of large fried-egg cells with clear cytoplasm, separated by fibrous bands full of lymphocytes. Its cells express placental alkaline phosphatase. Seminoma never makes AFP and can mildly raise hCG. It is very sensitive to radiation and chemotherapy and spreads late, so the prognosis is excellent.

Nonseminomatous germ cell tumors are usually mixed and more aggressive. **Embryonal carcinoma** is a hemorrhagic, necrotic mass of primitive cells that can be painful, and it may raise AFP or hCG. **Yolk sac tumor** is the most common testicular tumor in boys younger than 3. It secretes AFP and shows {{rp20schiller|Schiller-Duval bodies}}. **Choriocarcinoma**, made of syncytiotrophoblast and cytotrophoblast, spreads early through the blood to the lungs and brain, where its metastases can bleed. It makes very high hCG, which can cause gynecomastia and, by stimulating the TSH receptor, hyperthyroidism. Teratoma contains tissue from all three germ layers, and in adult men even mature-looking teratoma can metastasize.

Metastatic germ cell tumors, seminoma and nonseminoma alike, are treated with cisplatin-based chemotherapy, such as BEP (bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin). Cisplatin cross-links DNA and can injure the kidneys, inner ear and peripheral nerves. Bleomycin makes free radicals that break DNA and can cause pulmonary fibrosis and skin hyperpigmentation with little marrow suppression. Etoposide blocks topoisomerase II.

About 5 percent of testicular tumors arise from sex cord-stromal cells and make hormones rather than markers. A **Leydig cell tumor** is a golden-brown nodule of eosinophilic cells with rod-shaped {{rp20reinke|Reinke crystals}}. It makes androgens, which cause precocious puberty in boys, and some of these are converted to estrogen, which causes gynecomastia in men. AFP and hCG stay normal. Most are benign, and Sertoli cell tumors are usually hormonally silent. In men older than 60 the most common testicular mass is **lymphoma**, usually diffuse large B-cell type and often bilateral. Testicular tumors spread first to the **para-aortic** (retroperitoneal) lymph nodes, while choriocarcinoma spreads through the blood.
AFP normal; hCG normal or mildly raised
Tissue from all three germ layers
AFP raised in some; malignant potential in adult men
Working up a painless testicular lump
A firm mass within the testis that blocks light is treated as cancer until proven otherwise. A swelling that glows points to fluid.
Ultrasound confirms a solid intratesticular lesion and separates it from a hydrocele, spermatocele or varicocele outside the testis.
Markers drawn before surgery suggest the tumor type and give a baseline for follow-up after removal.
The testis and cord are removed through the groin, and a scrotal biopsy is avoided.
CT looks for spread to para-aortic nodes and lungs, and markers that fall more slowly than expected after surgery signal leftover tumor.
A high AFP means the tumor is not a pure seminoma

Pure seminoma never secretes **AFP**. If a tumor reported as seminoma comes with a raised AFP, it must contain a nonseminomatous part, usually yolk sac tumor. It is then treated as nonseminomatous. A mildly raised **hCG** fits seminoma, because scattered syncytiotrophoblast cells make it. Only very high hCG points to choriocarcinoma. LDH tracks tumor bulk, so it helps with prognosis, not with typing.
Why must a suspected testicular cancer be removed through the groin rather than the scrotum?

The testis develops near the kidney and drags its vessels and lymphatics with it as it descends. So its lymph drains to para-aortic nodes at the level of the renal vessels, while scrotal skin drains to superficial inguinal nodes. Cutting through the scrotum could spill tumor into the scrotal wall and open that second nodal route, which complicates staging and treatment. A radical inguinal orchiectomy removes the testis and cord through the groin and ties the cord high. The tumor therefore never touches the scrotal lymphatics.

body.q: A 61-year-old man has a new right-sided varicocele that stays full when he lies down. Which reasoning best guides the next step?
o: Right-sided varicoceles are the common kind because the right testicular vein is longer, so reassurance is enough
The right testicular vein drains straight into the inferior vena cava, so a new right varicocele that does not empty suggests a mass blocking venous return
A swelling that stays full when he is supine must be a hydrocele, so transillumination is the key test
Varicoceles come from arterial malformations, so Doppler of the testicular artery will settle the diagnosis
body.why: Varicoceles are usually left-sided because the left testicular vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle, giving a long, high-pressure column. The right vein enters the inferior vena cava at a gentle angle and rarely backs up. A new right-sided varicocele, or one that stays full lying flat, therefore implies a blockage downstream. The classic cause is renal cell carcinoma growing into the vena cava, so the abdomen is imaged.

grid.q: Which of these point toward testicular torsion rather than epididymitis?
items: High-riding testis with a horizontal lie
Bell-clapper attachment of the tunica vaginalis
Pain relieved by lifting the testis
Tender swollen epididymis with an intact reflex
